generated_summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a pathogen that causes respiratory, blood, liver, and bladder infections. This bacterium is a significant clinical concern due to its ability to infect multiple organs. The adaptor protein SKAP2 is required for protection against K. pneumoniae lung infections. SKAP2 helps the immune system defend the lungs from this bacterial infection. Mice lacking SKAP2 had 100-fold higher bacterial levels than normal mice during infection. SKAP2 expression in innate immune cells controlled the bacterial burden in these mice. Neutrophils without SKAP2 could not produce reactive oxygen species when exposed to K. pneumoniae. These neutrophils still degranulated normally despite the loss of reactive oxygen species production. Neutrophil reactive oxygen species production required the activity of SFKs, Syk, Btk, PLCγ2, and PKC. These proteins are key for neutrophils to respond to K. pneumoniae by producing reactive oxygen species. Loss of SKAP2 reduced activation of SFKs, Syk, and Pyk2 during K. pneumoniae infection. This shows SKAP2 acts early in the signaling pathway that activates these proteins. SKAP2 signaling in neutrophils is essential for reactive oxygen species production and bacterial clearance. This signaling helps the immune system control K. pneumoniae infections effectively.

The prevailing view in vertebrates is that BMP gradients form by a counter-gradient of BMP antagonists, sometimes with ligand shuttling. A counter-gradient means an opposing protein gradient inhibits BMP in certain areas. Researchers quantified the BMP activity gradient in wild-type and mutant zebrafish embryos at different developmental stages. They combined these data with a mathematical model-based computational screen to test gradient formation hypotheses. Zinski et al. used computer models to investigate how the BMP gradient is created. The analysis ruled out both a BMP shuttling mechanism and a bmp transcriptionally-informed gradient mechanism. This means BMP is not transported by shuttling proteins nor shaped only by bmp gene expression patterns. The analyses supported a source-sink mechanism where a restricted BMP antagonist distribution acts as a sink. This sink drives BMP flux dorsally and forms the BMP gradient instead of a counter-gradient. Measurements of Bmp2 diffusion in the zebrafish blastula supported the source-sink model for BMP gradient formation. Bmp2 spreads from its production site to the sink by diffusion during development. Measured Bmp2 diffusivity quantitatively matches predictions of the source-sink mechanism.

generated_summary: P2X receptors are ion channels that open a pore in response to extracellular ATP. This pore allows ions to pass through the cell membrane and start signals inside the cell. The mechanism of pore opening in P2X receptors is still controversial. More data are needed to understand how the full receptor opens in its natural membrane environment. This study used photo-switchable cross-linkers as molecular tweezers to monitor distances in the P2X2 receptor's transmembrane domain. These tweezers change length with light, allowing measurement of movements during receptor activation. Experimental constraints combined with computational studies created high-resolution models of the P2X2 channel in open and closed states. The outer pore expansion in P2X2 receptors is significantly reduced compared to the ATP-bound structure. This shows the open channel is more compact than previously thought. The inner and outer ends of adjacent pore-lining helices come closer during opening by a hinge-bending motion. This bending likely occurs at a critical gating hinge in the helices. These results provide new insight into the gating mechanism of P2X receptors. The method used is versatile and can be applied to study other membrane proteins.

generated_summary: Toxoplasma is an obligate intracellular parasite that replicates within a parasitophorous vacuole in mammalian cells. The parasitophorous vacuole does not fuse with other host organelles. This study examined how Toxoplasma exploits host lipid droplets, which are fat storage organelles. Toxoplasma replication is reduced in host cells depleted of lipid droplets or impaired in fat breakdown. This shows that host lipid droplets and their fat-processing are important for parasite growth. During infection, the parasitophorous vacuole is surrounded by host lipid droplets. Toxoplasma accesses lipids from host lipid droplets and uses them in its own membranes and lipid stores. Toxoplasma intercepts and internalizes host lipid droplets inside the vacuole to access their lipids. Some internalized droplets remain linked to Rab7 and are wrapped by a membrane network called IVN. Mutant parasites with defective IVN formation show reduced lipid uptake from host lipid droplets. This enzyme helps break down host lipid droplets to release lipids inside the vacuole. This study highlights Toxoplasma’s reliance on host lipid droplets for its intracellular development. The parasite is capable of scavenging neutral lipids from these host droplets.

Rhodamine B is a fluorescent dye that stains insect bodies and seminal fluid when fed in sugar. Rhodamine B is thiol-reactive, allowing it to bind body tissue and seminal fluid. This study adapted rhodamine B to mark male Aedes aegypti for rapid mating success assessment in field releases. Feeding males 0.1% to 0.8% rhodamine B in 50% honey for 4 days marked over 95% of bodies and transferred dye to over 95% of females. Rhodamine B marking did not affect male mating competitiveness and allowed transfer of marked seminal fluid to females in field tests. Field releases also showed marked males could be recaptured successfully. Rhodamine B is a useful evaluation method for male-based SIT/IIT control and a viable body marking technique without negative side-effects. Rhodamine B marking is less expensive and less time-consuming than PCR, stable isotope labelling, and female fertility assays for mating tests.

generated_summary: Reactive oxygen species (ROS) are produced in the mitochondrial respiratory chain (RC). ROS act as signals for cell adaptation and can also damage cells under stress like hypoxia/reoxygenation. Understanding how ROS are produced is important for cell survival. Details of the mechanisms and factors controlling ROS production remain unclear. Researchers extended a model of complex III to include the whole respiratory chain and related processes. The model covers electron transport, proton movement, electrochemical potential, TCA cycle, and substrate transport. The model fits electron flux data from rat brain mitochondria fueled by succinate or pyruvate and malate. It also reproduces NAD+ reduction dynamics via reverse electron transport through complex I. The model explains how free radicals form and transfer electrons to oxygen, starting ROS production. Free radicals create superoxide by passing unpaired electrons to oxygen molecules. ROS production is linked to specific free radicals in complexes I and III of the respiratory chain. Different radicals from electron transporters contribute to ROS levels in these complexes. Bistability, seen before in complex III, also occurs in the whole respiratory chain. This means the chain can stably exist in two states with different ROS levels under the same conditions. Conditions causing complex III to switch to high free radical levels were predicted and confirmed experimentally. Changes like increased succinate or temporary hypoxia can trigger this switch to higher ROS production. These findings provide new insight into how ROS are produced in the mitochondrial respiratory chain.

generated_summary: Diagnosis and treatment are crucial for controlling human African trypanosomiasis (HAT). HAT is caused mainly by the parasite Trypanosoma brucei gambiense. Current rapid diagnostic tests (RDTs) use native antigens that are difficult to produce. Producing native antigens requires a costly and risky process involving live parasites. This study evaluated a new RDT called SD BIOLINE HAT 2.0 using recombinant antigens. Recombinant antigens are easier and safer to manufacture than native antigens. The study screened 57,632 people in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Screening was done passively at health centers and actively by mobile teams, confirming 260 HAT cases by parasitology. SD BIOLINE HAT 2.0 had the highest sensitivity at 71.2%, outperforming CATT and SD BIOLINE HAT. CATT was the most specific test with 99.2% specificity. SD BIOLINE HAT and SD BIOLINE HAT 2.0 had specificities of 98.9% and 98.1%, respectively. Combining SD BIOLINE HAT with SD BIOLINE HAT 2.0 increased sensitivity to 98.4% in passive screening. Combination also improved sensitivity to 83.0% in active screening. Using two or more tests improves sensitivity but slightly reduces specificity. Further research is needed on the practicality and cost-effectiveness of combined screening.

generated_summary: Many NTD-endemic countries cannot start or expand programs due to lack of baseline data. Baseline data are needed for planning and advocacy of public health programs. An integrated mapping approach can save resources where NTDs overlap geographically. NTDs often affect the same areas, so combining mapping efforts reduces costs. Researchers developed and tested the Integrated Threshold Mapping (ITM) protocol for four NTDs. The four diseases are lymphatic filariasis, trachoma, schistosomiasis, and soil-transmitted helminths. The ITM protocol identifies if disease levels reach thresholds to trigger interventions. It is designed to be resource-efficient and works at the implementation unit level. The ITM protocol was tested against WHO methods in one district each in Mali and Senegal. The comparison covered all four targeted diseases using current WHO mapping guidelines. ITM agreed with WHO methods on interventions for trachoma, LF, and STH. For schistosomiasis, ITM gave more targeted intervention recommendations. The integrated mapping tool could help implement needed NTD programs in endemic countries.

feedback_items.fact: YKU80 and TLC1 were validated as telomere-length QTLs in two S. paradoxus subpopulations using reciprocal hemizygosity.
feedback_items.source_span: We validated by reciprocal hemizygosity that YKU80 and TLC1 are telomere-length QTLs in the two S . paradoxus subpopulations . We confirmed that part of the variation in telomere length among individuals is due to natural sequence variants within YKU80 and TLC1 . The segregant analysis suggested that the YKU80 marker was strongly linked with the telomere length phenotype ( LOD 5 . 34 , variance explained 12% ) with length averages of 370 bp and 276 bp for the spores carrying the YPS or the CBS allele respectively ( Table S2 ) . Similarly , we validated the quantitative effect on telomere length of TLC1 ( LOD 4 . 25 , variance explained 9 . 74% ) by reciprocal hemizygosity ( Figure 5B ) .

generated_summary: Proteins often perform their biological functions through collective atomic motions. These motions include hinge movements, domain rotations, and side chain rearrangements. Identifying collective motions related to a specific protein function from molecular dynamics trajectories is often difficult. Molecular dynamics simulations track protein movements but linking them to function is challenging. A new technique called functional mode analysis (FMA) detects collective motions linked to a protein function. FMA analyzes protein structure ensembles to find motions related to function. FMA uses an ensemble of structures and a functional quantity to find the motion most correlated to function. The functional quantity measures the protein's functional state in various ways. The functional quantity can be geometric, electrostatic, chemical, or any variable relevant to protein function. FMA also estimates the motion most likely to cause a large change in the functional quantity. This motion is called the ensemble-weighted most correlated motion (ewMCM). FMA applies Pearson correlation for linear relations and mutual information for any interdependence. Using both measures detects simple and complex links between motion and function. The FMA approach is demonstrated on biomolecules like polyalanine-helix, T4 lysozyme, Trp-cage, and leucine-binding protein.

generated_summary: Coxsackievirus B (CVB) usually causes a mild fever in infants but can cause acute myocarditis. CVB is an enterovirus that commonly causes this self-limited febrile illness. The long-term effects of mild CVB infection are unknown despite links to late heart failure. There is an epidemiologic association between early subclinical infections and later heart failure. A mouse model infected as juveniles with a low dose of CVB3 showed no symptoms immediately or in adulthood. The infection dose was subclinical, causing no obvious disease signs in the mice. After cardiac stress, juvenile-infected adult mice developed heart enlargement and dilation. These changes indicate progression toward heart failure in the stressed mice. Normally, stressed adult hearts increase CD31+ blood vessel formation, but this was suppressed in juvenile-infected mice. CVB3 infected juvenile c-kit+ cardiac progenitor cells and reduced their numbers in adult hearts. C-kit+ cells are heart progenitor cells important for repair and growth. The reduced progenitor cell pool may impair the heart's ability to increase capillary density under stress. This impairment limits the heart's adaptation to increased workload after juvenile CVB3 infection.

generated_summary: The filarial nematode Brugia malayi causes Lymphatic Filariasis. Parasitic nematodes like B. malayi can change host biology, but how is unclear. Parasites release extracellular vesicles (EVs) carrying proteins and small RNAs to affect hosts. Extracellular vesicles are tiny sacs that carry molecules from parasites to host tissues. This study measured EV release from all mammal-stage Brugia malayi forms. These forms include microfilariae, L3, L4, and adult male and female worms. EV release is a secretory process conserved across the Brugia malayi life cycle. Nanoparticle Tracking Analysis showed distinct EV populations at all stages. Brugia EVs are taken up by mouse macrophages equally from all life stages. Macrophages are immune cells that internalize EVs without stage preference. All Brugia EVs enter macrophages through phagocytosis. Chemical inhibitors showed that macrophages engulf EVs by phagocytosis. Protein analysis found male and female Brugia EVs differ in immune-related cargo. These differences suggest sex-specific roles in modulating the host immune response. Ivermectin quickly reduces EV release from all Brugia malayi life stages. The drug inhibited EV release by 44% to 82% depending on the stage. Ivermectin also blocks EV release in the related nematode Dirofilaria immitis. This effect was absent in an ivermectin-resistant Dirofilaria strain.

feedback_items.fact: There is currently no direct genetic evidence to support the foundational model that suberin forms a chemical barrier limiting extracellular transport of water and solutes in plant roots.
feedback_items.source_span: Though central to our understanding of how roots perform their vital function of scavenging water and solutes from the soil , no direct genetic evidence currently exists to support the foundational model that suberin acts to form a chemical barrier limiting the extracellular , or apoplastic , transport of water and solutes in plant roots . A long held model to explain this regulation includes the function of the extracellular biopolymer suberin acting as a barrier to limit the apoplastic transport of water and solutes . The size of stomatal openings affects photosynthesis, water use, and crop yields. Opening size influences how efficiently plants use water and produce food. Modification of HRB1 by PP7 under blue light is essential for forming a functional HRB1 protein complex. This modification helps HRB1 adopt the right shape or recruit other components. This study may help develop strategies for plants to better survive water shortage. It could improve both constant and stress-induced plant protections.

generated_summary: Combination chemotherapy with oral rifampicin and intramuscular streptomycin improved Buruli ulcer treatment. This treatment also reduced recurrence rates of the disease. Wound healing is delayed in some antibiotic-treated Buruli ulcer patients for unclear reasons. Immunohistochemical investigations were done to find markers for monitoring wound healing. Tissue samples from eight patients were analyzed before, during, and after chemotherapy. The analysis focused on markers of tissue formation, remodeling, and skin activation. Alpha-smooth muscle actin positive myofibroblasts appeared during the healing process. These cells were absent in untreated lesions but emerged as healing progressed. Myofibroblasts produced extracellular matrix proteins like pro-collagen 1 and tenascin. These proteins were found in areas rich in fibronectin. After antibiotic treatment, many cells showed activation with ribosomal protein S6 phosphorylation. This activation included myofibroblasts and indicates increased protein production. Healing wounds showed tissue remodeling by apoptosis and increased cytokeratin 16 in the epidermis. Apoptosis is programmed cell death, and cytokeratin 16 indicates skin cell growth. This marker panel may help understand causes of delayed wound healing in some patients. The markers allow assessment of tissue repair progression and functional disturbances.

This study examined inflammatory mediators and endothelial cell-intrinsic pathways in NS1-induced vascular leak. The goal was to see if inflammation or direct cell effects cause the leak. DENV NS1, but not West Nile virus NS1, triggers localized vascular leak in wild-type mice. This shows vascular leak is specific to DENV NS1 among related viruses. Human dermal endothelial cells exposed to DENV NS1 do not produce inflammatory cytokines. Blocking cytokines TNF-α, IL-6, and IL-8 does not reduce NS1-induced leak. DENV NS1 causes vascular leak in mice lacking TLR4 or TNF-α receptors at levels like normal mice. This indicates inflammatory signaling via TLR4 and TNF-α is not required for leak. Inhibitors targeting glycocalyx-disrupting molecules block DENV NS1-induced vascular leak in vivo. These inhibitors prevent enzymes that break down the glycocalyx layer. DENV NS1-induced vascular leak depends on endothelial glycocalyx components, not inflammatory cytokines.

generated_summary: The PR interval on an electrocardiogram reflects conduction time in the atria and atrioventricular node. It measures the time for electrical impulses to travel through these heart regions. Genome-wide association studies have found genetic factors for PR interval in Europeans and Asians but are limited in African ancestry. This study performed genome-wide association studies in 6,247 African American individuals from four cohorts. The goal was to find genetic variants linked to PR interval duration. A strong genetic signal (rs3922844) was found in the SCN5A gene with genome-wide significance in African Americans. SCN5A encodes the cardiac sodium channel important for heart function. The rs3922844 variant explained 2% of PR interval variability in African Americans. The same variant was linked to PR interval in Europeans but explained only 0.5% of variability with a smaller effect. The difference in effect size between ancestries was statistically significant. Meta-analysis found significant associations with SNPs in SCN10A, MEIS1, and TBX5, matching European and Asian studies. Common genetic variants at four loci are relevant to African Americans and include a stronger SCN5A association than in Europeans.

generated_summary: Many U.S.-bound refugees come from countries where intestinal parasites are common. These parasites include hookworm, Trichuris trichuria, Ascaris lumbricoides, and Strongyloides stercoralis. Intestinal parasite infections are rare in the United States and may be underdiagnosed or misdiagnosed. This can lead to serious health problems for refugees. The study compared costs and benefits of overseas treatment, domestic screening, and no program. These strategies target parasitic diseases in U.S.-bound refugees. Researchers used an economic decision tree model with Markov processes for 27,700 Asian refugees. The model estimated costs and health impacts of four interventions. Overseas albendazole and ivermectin treatment costs less than domestic screening or combined approaches. It is cheaper than domestic screening and treatment or overseas albendazole plus domestic screening for Strongyloides. Overseas albendazole and ivermectin reduces outpatient cases, deaths, and hospitalizations by about 80%. The cost per quality-adjusted life year gained is $2,219 compared to no program. Overseas presumptive treatment is cost-effective and at least as effective as domestic screening programs. It costs less and achieves better or equal health outcomes than screening after arrival. Adding ivermectin to albendazole lowers chronic strongyloidiasis and fatal disseminated strongyloidiasis risks. This reduces long-term infections and rare deadly complications in refugees.

The infection is asymptomatic in these rats, which carry the bacteria in their kidneys. Wild rodents, including the brown rat (Rattus norvegicus), are the main reservoirs of Leptospira. Understanding rat-to-rat transmission requires studying natural infection routes like mucosal or subcutaneous inoculation. This study compared subcutaneous and mucosal inoculation routes to the intraperitoneal route in adult rats. Leptospira infection was asymptomatic in rats regardless of the inoculation route. All rats produced similar antibody levels despite differences in kidney colonization. Renal colonization occurred in all rats after intraperitoneal infection, in five of eight after mucosal, and in one of eight after subcutaneous infection. Mucosal inoculation was more efficient than subcutaneous for kidney colonization and urinary excretion. These results improve understanding of Leptospira infection in rats. The findings clarify infection modalities beyond epidemiological studies in wild rats.

generated_summary: The study focused on insulin receptors (SjIRs) in Schistosoma japonicum to explore insulin signaling's role in parasite growth and reproduction. Mice were challenged with a low dose of S. japonicum to test vaccine effects. The results support SjIRs as veterinary transmission-blocking vaccine candidates against schistosomiasis japonica in China and the Philippines. Targeting SjIRs could help control parasite spread from animal reservoirs to humans.

generated_summary: In humans, reinfections by Trypanosoma cruzi may worsen chronic Chagas disease symptoms. However, the frequency and timing of these reinfections are not well known. The models were fitted to data from Argentinean rural villages with 56% mixed infections. Mixed infections mean people carry different parasite genotypes at once. Low reinfection rates are mainly due to weak stercorarian transmission efficiency. This transmission occurs when parasites enter through insect feces. These reinfection estimates are important for vaccine development and understanding chronic disease risks in endemic areas.

generated_summary: Most dengue virus (DENV) infections are subclinical but prior immunity can affect later disease outcome. Subclinical infections cause mild or no symptoms, while later infections can be more severe. The mechanisms behind different clinical outcomes of DENV infection are not well understood. Immune cells from these samples were exposed to DENV in the lab and 30 cytokines were measured. The cells tested were peripheral blood mononuclear cells, or PBMC. These differences support the existence of both protective and pathologic immune profiles in DENV infection. Higher levels of some cytokines were found in symptomatic subjects, others in subclinical cases. These immune patterns may help evaluate responses to dengue vaccines.

generated_summary: Polygenic type 2 diabetes in mouse models is linked to obesity and involves adipogenic and diabetogenic alleles. A candidate gene was identified for the diabetogenic effect of the QTL Nidd/SJL from SJL, NON, and NZB strains. This gene was found in crosses with New Zealand Obese (NZO) mice. A 2.1 Mbp critical interval on distal chromosome 4 was linked to the diabetic phenotype. This region was identified by introgressing SJL segments into diabetes-resistant C57BL/6J mice and crossing with NZO mice. Analysis of 10 genes in this interval showed a strong allelic difference in Zfp69, encoding zinc finger domain transcription factor 69. In NZO and C57BL/6J mice, a retrotransposon IAPLTR1a disrupts Zfp69 by creating a truncated mRNA missing KRAB and Znf-C2H2 domains. Diabetogenic alleles from SJL, NON, and NZB produce a normal full-length mRNA. The diabetogenic Zfp69SJL allele causes hyperglycaemia, less gonadal fat, and higher plasma and liver triglycerides in B6.V-Lepob mice. The human equivalent gene ZNF642 shows increased mRNA levels in fat tissue from type 2 diabetes patients. Zfp69 is the most likely gene causing the diabetogenic effect of Nidd/SJL. The retrotransposon IAPLTR1a contributes to genetic differences among mouse strains. Expression of Zfp69 in fat tissue may play a role in type 2 diabetes development.

candidate_summaries.summary: Polygenic type 2 diabetes in mouse models is linked to obesity and involves adipogenic and diabetogenic alleles. A candidate gene was identified for the diabetogenic effect of the QTL Nidd/SJL from SJL, NON, and NZB strains. This gene was found in crosses with New Zealand Obese (NZO) mice. A 2.1 Mbp critical interval on distal chromosome 4 was linked to the diabetic phenotype. This region was identified by introgressing SJL segments into diabetes-resistant C57BL/6J mice and crossing with NZO mice. Analysis of 10 genes in this interval showed a strong allelic difference in Zfp69, encoding zinc finger domain transcription factor 69. In NZO and C57BL/6J mice, a retrotransposon IAPLTR1a disrupts Zfp69 by creating a truncated mRNA missing KRAB and Znf-C2H2 domains. Diabetogenic alleles from SJL, NON, and NZB produce a normal full-length mRNA. The diabetogenic Zfp69SJL allele causes hyperglycaemia, less gonadal fat, and higher plasma and liver triglycerides in B6.V-Lepob mice. The human equivalent gene ZNF642 shows increased mRNA levels in fat tissue from type 2 diabetes patients. Zfp69 is the most likely gene causing the diabetogenic effect of Nidd/SJL. The retrotransposon IAPLTR1a contributes to genetic differences among mouse strains. Expression of Zfp69 in fat tissue may play a role in type 2 diabetes development.

candidate_summaries.summary: Mathematical modeling and sensitivity analysis can find fragile points in human biological cascades. These fragile points are sensitive mechanisms that could serve as therapeutic targets. The study tested this idea by screening a mathematical model of the coagulation cascade. The coagulation cascade is a well-studied process involved in blood clotting. The model included 92 proteins and 148 protein interactions and was validated with 21 published datasets. These datasets came from two different in vitro coagulation models. Simulated platelet activation and thrombin generation matched measured values with a mean correlation of 0.87. Overall state sensitivity coefficients were calculated using a Monte Carlo strategy to measure mechanism fragility. These coefficients show how sensitive each mechanism is to changes in the model. Without anticoagulants, factor X activity and thrombin-driven platelet activation were fragile mechanisms. Factor IX and factor VIII activation and activity were robust and less sensitive to change. Anti-factor X and direct thrombin inhibitors are key anticoagulants with FDA approval for preventing blood clots. These results support using computationally found fragile points to select therapeutic targets despite model uncertainty.

Mediator is a protein complex that helps activate genes, and H3K27ac marks active enhancers. About 15% of combinatorial binding events and up to 63% at early developmental enhancers are conserved between species. Combined OCT4, SOX2, and NANOG binding is critical for transcription and important for embryogenesis at conserved enhancers. Fast evolutionary changes mainly affect individual binding, while multi-factor hotspots are under stronger constraints. These hotspots are active in multiple tissues during early development and resist evolutionary change.

Passive transfer of convalescent human plasma shows promise as a treatment for HPS. However, plasma from survivors is very limited in availability. This tested protection in a lethal HPS hamster model. Both immune sera and purified IgY/IgYΔFc from vaccinated geese protected most hamsters from lethal HPS. Eight of eight hamsters survived with immune sera, and seven of eight with purified antibodies. All hamsters given antibodies from normal geese or no treatment developed lethal HPS. This shows protection was specific to antibodies from vaccinated geese. The DNA vaccine/goose platform can produce antiviral biologics that prevent lethal HPS when given post-exposure.

generated_summary: Current drugs for Chagas disease have toxic effects and only partly work. These medicines target only the acute phase of the disease. No drug is available to treat the chronic stage of Chagas disease. Researchers optimized a whole cell-based assay to screen compounds blocking Trypanosoma cruzi infection. This method tests many compounds for their ability to stop the parasite infecting mammalian cells. A 2000-compound chemical library was screened using a recombinant T. cruzi strain expressing β-galactosidase. The enzyme helps detect parasite growth during screening. Three compounds—PCH1, NT1, and CX1—showed high activity against T. cruzi and low toxicity in vitro. Their IC50 values were 54, 190, and 23 nM, respectively. Each compound acts differently on the intracellular growth of T. cruzi amastigotes. CX1 has strong trypanocidal activity, killing parasites inside cells. This is important for treating the chronic stage where parasites are dormant inside cells. NT1 stops parasite growth without killing, while PCH1 disrupts parasite division. The three compounds also work against T. cruzi Y strain and related parasites Leishmania major and L. amazonensis. Two related compounds, PCH6 and CX2, showed improved activity with IC50 values of 2 nM. These IC50 values are about 100 times lower than those of current medicines for T. cruzi. These results provide new candidate molecules for treating Chagas disease and leishmaniasis.

Chronic musculoskeletal pain lasts months to years after CHIKV infection in many patients. The cause of this long-lasting pain is not well understood. Jobs linked to higher risk were rice farming, fishing, and animal breeding. Praziquantel treatment, access to sanitation, and living farther from freshwater reduced infection risk. Environmental factors mainly shaped infection patterns with low risk in mountains and high risk in the Mekong corridor. This study provides the first risk map of O. viverrini infection in Champasack province. The map helps target control efforts to high-risk areas.
